Distortion

/dih-STOR-shuhn/ - the stress falls on STOR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Distortion means a twisting of facts or meaning that misrepresents the truth.

By the third retelling, the account of the missed penalty had picked up a distortion: now the goalie had 'taunted the crowd,' something no one at the game had seen.

Worked Example

The mayor's flyer warned that her opponent 'wants to shut down our parks.' His actual proposal trimmed summer hours at two of the city's forty parks to pay for lifeguards at the pool. The claim grew from something real—hours were indeed being cut—which is exactly what made the distortion effective.

Distortion is the right word, rather than 'lie,' because a lie is built from nothing while a distortion starts from the truth and bends it: the facts stay recognizable, just twisted out of shape.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

misrepresentation: a false or misleading account, whether intentional or careless

spin: a slanted, self-serving framing of true facts—an informal word

half-truth: a statement accurate as far as it goes and misleading for what it omits

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

accuracy: an account that matches the facts as they are

honesty: truthfulness as a personal habit

Where it sits · how far the account departs from fact — slant → distortion → fabrication

slant vs. distortion: A slant tilts the emphasis—good news first, bad news buried—while a distortion twists the facts themselves out of shape.

fabrication vs. distortion: Fabrication goes past distortion: a distortion bends something that really happened, while a fabrication is manufactured from nothing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart, in different directions

Root — tort

Root — tort: to twist

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Dis- (apart) + tort (to twist) + -ion (result of) = the result of twisting apart. Latin torquere, 'to twist,' gives English a whole family of wrenched and warped things, and distortion applies the twisting to facts: the events stay recognizable, but their shape has been wrung until they say something untrue.

Use the root in a new word: contort

Use the root in a new word: contort: The escape artist can contort his shoulders enough to slip out of a buckled straitjacket.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / analytical

Distortion accuses an account of bending real facts—stronger than spin, weaker than outright fabrication. Its neighbors in this unit divide the territory: a spurious document is fake from the start, a fallacious argument breaks down in its logic, and a distortion takes true material and twists it. You will also meet its adjective cousin, distorted, in this unit's exercises.
